title: Finish rebrand, then test the contract
input: I'm a freelance designer and this month is a mess. A client wants a full rebrand by the 20th. Two old clients owe me invoices. I keep meaning to raise my rates, and my portfolio site is three years old. Someone offered me a part-time agency contract that pays steady but would eat two days a week. I also want to learn motion design. What do I do first, what waits, and should I take the agency contract?

out.title: Sort a crowded freelance month
out.summary: One hard deadline (rebrand by the 20th), money owed, three slow goals (rates, portfolio, motion), and one big decision (agency contract, two days a week). Rates, portfolio and motion can wait, but a rate rise for new work costs nothing to start.

out.summary: Opportunity cost view: the rebrand (25 hours, hard deadline) and the overdue invoices come first because they are the cheapest money and the biggest loss if missed. The agency contract's real cost is two days a week of your day rate, but with a 1-3 month runway, steady income likely beats the gap. Don't decide yet: ask about motion work and start date this week, then negotiate a start after the 20th. Rates, portfolio and motion learning wait.

out.summary: Second-order view: finish the rebrand first, chase the two invoices this week, and treat the agency contract as likely yes but only after you ask about start date, pay and motion work. The contract's steady pay fixes your thin runway. Its cost is two days a week, which squeezes the rate rise, the portfolio and motion learning. Those can wait and mostly cannot be done in parallel.

findings.text: You stated runway is 1-3 months, the invoices total about one month of costs, and the rebrand has about 25 hours left.
You stated the contract is six months fixed, 30 days notice, steady, below your day rate, about two days a week.

Rebrand first: missing the 20th risks the payment, a referral source and a reference. Those losses would hit the weakest cash position you have. 25 hours is about 3-4 working days, so it fits if protected.

Chasing the invoices is cheap (an hour or two) and could add a month of runway. If paid, the contract becomes a choice rather than a need. If ignored, the cash gap stays and pushes you to accept worse terms.

Taking the contract: money steadies, then two days a week are gone. Remaining capacity is about three days. New client work shrinks, so your income depends on the lower contract rate more than you may want.
Declining the contract: you keep full capacity for higher-rate work, but with 1-3 months runway, one slow month forces a worse decision later. Reversing is hard because the offer may not return.
A rate rise has a second-order cost under the contract: with fewer open days, you can afford to lose small clients over price. So the contract makes the rate rise safer for new quotes.
Portfolio work done now gets little use if you are about to be busy. Done during the contract, it feeds higher-rate work later. Order matters less than doing it once.
If the agency does motion work, the contract may also pay you to learn. If not, motion learning competes for the same hours and slips to later.
The contract pay still covers your monthly costs together with some freelance income. This is untested.
The rebrand client pays on time. The old invoices suggest late payment is possible in your client base.
